blocks.text: 负载均衡
由于我们不在代理中存储会话状态，会话状态的权威视图仅存在于拥有该会话的主机上。这意味着负载均衡器无法即时获得可用容量的全局视图。

inlines.text: 由于我们不在代理中存储会话状态，会话状态的权威视图仅存在于拥有该会话的主机上。这意味着负载均衡器无法即时获得可用容量的全局视图。

blocks.text: 为了发现可用容量，我们的负载均衡器会定期探测容器，以获取其可用并发数的快照。然后，负载均衡器结合最近的路由决策和探测到的快照来选择容器。这会将会话均匀分布到可用容器上，同时尽量减少向容量不足的容器发送浪费的往返请求。

blocks.text: 自动扩缩容

blocks.text: Serverless with strong affinity

Modal has supported WebSockets via Web Functions for some time. However, a WebSocket connection is tied to a Function “input”, not a container—if the connection drops, a new input is created on reconnect and can land on a different container.

blocks.text: Stateful web UIs such as Gradio and Streamlit are workloads that need strong affinity guarantees between requests and backend containers. Every request has to reach the process that holds the user’s state. One anti-pattern workaround is setting max_containers=1, which guarantees stickiness by giving up scaling entirely.

blocks.text: Sticky Sessions build on the infrastructure we developed for Modal Servers. At the core of this infrastructure is our in-house stateless proxy (fprs). The proxy provides low-latency routing and load balancing using in-memory cached routing state reconciled from durable storage. Servers already give us a way to route HTTP traffic to a container, manage container lifecycles, and scale the fleet based on demand.

blocks.text: Sticky Sessions needed three things that the current request-level routing didn’t provide:

inlines.text: Sticky Sessions needed three things that the current request-level routing didn’t provide:
Every request in a session reaches the same container.
The container’s host tracks which requests belong to which sessions and determines when each session becomes idle.
The container fleet scales with the number of active sessions rather than requests.

blocks.text: Making serverless infrastructure session-aware
From the client’s perspective, a Sticky Session works like a pipe. Once the client creates a session, every future request for that session will be directed to the same container.

blocks.text: This may seem simple, but Modal’s serverless infrastructure was built and optimized for the opposite idea; that individual requests are independent. In viewing Modal Servers from the perspective of sessions (rather than just requests), we had to reason about authorization, load balancing, and autoscaling from first principles.

blocks.text: Authorization
Modal Servers require Proxy Tokens by default. To share Sticky Sessions, you shouldn’t need to turn off authentication or pass your Proxy Token around.

blocks.text: Instead, each sessions.start() request returns a signed session token to grant access to that session. Sharing this token among clients lets multiple participants access the same state in a room, game, or collaborative app.

blocks.text: Maintaining the session-to-container mapping in the proxy would require keeping that mapping consistent through restarts and across multiple replicas. To avoid this, we encode routing metadata directly into the token. Our proxies validate the token and route requests to the container holding the session.

inlines.text: Maintaining the session-to-container mapping in the proxy would require keeping that mapping consistent through restarts and across multiple replicas. To avoid this, we encode routing metadata directly into the token. Our proxies validate the token and route requests to the container holding the session.

blocks.text: Load Balancing

Since we’re not storing session state in the proxy, the authoritative view of session state lives only on the host that owns the session. This means the load balancer cannot have an instantaneous global view of available capacity.

inlines.text: Since we’re not storing session state in the proxy, the authoritative view of session state lives only on the host that owns the session. This means the load balancer cannot have an instantaneous global view of available capacity.

blocks.text: To discover available capacity, our load balancers periodically probe containers for a snapshot of their available concurrency. The load balancers then use a combination of recent routing decisions and the probed snapshots to inform container selection. This evenly distributes sessions across available containers while minimizing wasted roundtrips to containers that are out of capacity.

The load balancers then use a combination of recent routing decisions and the probed snapshots to inform container selection. This evenly distributes sessions across available containers while minimizing wasted roundtrips to containers that are out of capacity.

blocks.text: Autoscaling

Modal Servers autoscale on request volume, aiming to achieve a per-container request concurrency target. The request-driven autoscaler assumes that request traffic can be rebalanced evenly across the serving fleet of containers. This model works well for stateless Servers. However, Sticky Sessions behave differently in that session traffic is not movable. Each session’s traffic has to land on the same container even if traffic volume varies across sessions.

blocks.text: This motivated having sessions be the unit of concurrency, akin to Modal Functions with inputs. A container can be configured to run 1 or more sessions concurrently. When concurrency runs out, new sessions wait in a queue for existing sessions to end or a new container to become ready. The autoscaler continuously monitors active session counts and queued demand to make scaling decisions that appropriately size the compute fleet.

blocks.text: Shared rooms: Our sessioned chat room example backs each chat room with a Sticky Session. Every client that connects with the session token is routed to the same container. Each room’s messages are broadcasted to everyone in the room. Clients can drop and reconnect to the same room for the lifetime of the chat room session.
